            PROTEST OF THE INDEPENDENT MARKET MONITOR FOR PJM

          Pursuant to Rules 211 of the Commission’s Rules and Regulations, 1 Monitoring

Analytics, LLC, acting in its capacity as the Independent Market Monitor (“Market Monitor”)

for PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), 2 submits this protest of the filing on July 15, 2026

(“July 15th Filing”), requesting approval of a proposed transaction (“Transaction” or

“Merger”) under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act in which NextEra Energy, Inc.

(“NextEra”) will acquire Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion” and, together with NextEra,

the “Applicants”). 3 According to NextEra, the Merger will create the “largest power company

and third largest company in the energy sector in the United States” and “number one in

America in total power generation, the world's leader in renewables and energy storage,

America's number one gas generator and second largest nuclear generator,” also combining

 two vertically integrated utilities in four Southeast states, each with captive rate payers. 4 Both

companies have generation, transmission, and distribution assets as part of their regulated

utilities. The Merger also involves merchant generation, merchant transmission, and natural

gas pipelines. Both companies are highly involved in serving current and future data center

load. The Merger would result in an unprecedented amount of economic and political power

for NextEra. The Commission’s standard merger review process does not contemplate all of

the implications of the Merger. The potential harms to the public interest include deterrence

of potential competition, control of inputs to production, control of access to customers, rent

seeking, expansion of monopoly power, incentives for further increases in the concentration

of asset ownership in PJM, and potential impacts on PJM’s governance. 5

       The July 15th Filing fails to address increases in market power created by the Merger.

The July 15th Filing should be rejected. The July 15th Filing (at 2) states that “over the longer

term, the combined company’s scale, financial strength, and operational breadth is likely to

yield customer benefits.” The July 15th Filing fails to explain how this “likely” result could

occur over the longer term and how long the longer term is. The July 15th Filing provides no

mechanism that would result in long term customer benefits. The July 15th Filing does not

define the relevant customers in this claim. Scale, financial strength, and operational breadth

all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors

rather than customers. The Applicants have not asserted that this Merger enhances

competition or market efficiency. The Applicants have not explained why the Merger is

Power Act requires a finding that it is consistent with the public interest. Although Section

203 has been interpreted not to require Applicants to show benefits to the public interest, it

cannot be approved if concerns about harm to competition are supported with evidence in

the record, and those concerns are not mitigated. 7 The Merger cannot be approved “on

balance,” where on balance the transaction is harmful because the Applicants do not show

that benefits offset unmitigated harms. 8 In this case, Applicants show no offsetting benefits.

The Merger cannot be approved, including on balance, without a finding that benefits to the

public interest offset the harm identified in the record. 9 Applicants have not explained why

the Merger is consistent with the public interest.

whether the Merger is in the public interest, given that competitive markets are relied upon

application was incomplete and insufficient to assess changes in structural market power. 11

Applicants provide results showing no HHI screen failures for the PJM market. The Market

Monitor’s attached market power analysis shows that the Merger would result in small

increases in structural market power relative to Dominion’s current market power and

dominant market position in PJM and based on existing assets under historic market

conditions. The analysis also shows that NextEra would purchase market power and that

NextEra’s market power in the PJM markets would increase significantly.

       Equally or more important impacts of the Merger are the elimination of a significant

competitor in generation and transmission, deterrence of potential competition from smaller,

innovative potential entrants, control of inputs to production, control of access to customers,

rent seeking, expansion of monopoly power, the incentive for other very large competitors to

engage in further acquisitions to keep pace with the merged company with the result being

a greater concentration of asset ownership in PJM markets, and potential impacts on PJM’s

governance.

I. COMMENTS

       A. The Harm to Competition Due to the Merger Requires Consideration of
          Competitive Effects that Cannot be Measured by Traditional Metrics.

       The competitive effects of the Merger extend far beyond the change in HHI or the

change in pivotal supplier metrics based on the existing generation assets owned by NextEra

and Dominion in the PJM market. As the Department of Justice and Federal Trade

Commission pointed out in their comments on the Commission’s merger guidelines:

“Structural measures, such as market shares and market concentration, should be the starting

owner of capacity in the constrained Chesapeake submarket, which includes Northern

Virginia’s Data Center Alley and the Baltimore-Washington D.C. metropolitan area. 15

NextEra already has plans to build at least 4.3 GW of generation in PJM, particularly in

the rapidly evolving changes. This combination of existing and future assets, along with

 Dominion’s market position with access to captive customers, a regulated rate base and the

largest concentration of current data center load and future data center load growth in PJM,

creates a significant threat to competition in the PJM markets. Applicants’ limited market

power analysis does not and cannot adequately account for all the horizontal and vertical

competitive effects, including immediate and future, this Merger would create in the PJM

market alone.

       The screens required by the Commission’s Merger Policy Statement do not

definitively determine whether a merger will cause harm to the public interest. 19 In 2023, the

Department of Justice and Federal Trade Commission antitrust agencies adopted new merger

guidelines that emphasize the importance of considering harm to competition that goes

beyond static measures of market concentration. 20 The Agency Guidelines state that:
                Mergers that substantially lessen competition or tend to create a
                monopoly increase, extend, or entrench market power and deprive
                the public of these benefits [of competition]. Mergers can lessen
                competition when they diminish competitive constraints, reduce
                the number or attractiveness of alternatives available to trading
                partners, or reduce the intensity with which market participants
                compete. 21

       The Merger of NextEra and Dominion, would reduce competition by eliminating a

competitive merchant generator and a competitive transmission company in the PJM market,

by reducing competition from alternative suppliers of new thermal generation, new

renewable generation, new energy storage resources in Virginia, by eliminating a competitor

creating an incentive for further increases in the concentration of asset ownership in PJM.

Each of these causes of competitive harm can be tied to one or more of the enumerated

Agency Guidelines, which identify the various ways a merger can harm competition. 22

               1. The Merger will Reduce Competition from New Entry and Remove an
                  Active Competitor in the PJM Market.

       The Applicants’ static and traditional market power analysis in the July 15th Filing

relies on a view of markets from before competitive wholesale power markets existed, fails

to consider the actual current and evolving competitive environment, and fails to look

forward and recognize the effects on the incentives for the entry of new, innovative,

competitive suppliers of generation and transmission in PJM and other markets.

       Economists have long recognized the incentive and ability of a large incumbent firm

(or “first mover”) to deter entry in a market using its access to capital, information, or cost

advantages to signal a competitive advantage that would limit the profitability of its potential

competitors. 23 The competitors, receiving the signal of lower potential profits for themselves,

scale back their plans or do not enter the market, leaving higher profits for the large

incumbent. Industries with economies of scale and barriers to entry, like electric power, are

more vulnerable to this exercise of market power. NextEra has claimed competitive

advantages due to the Merger, including taking advantage of their regulated business with

ratepayer guaranteed returns on investments, enhanced access to credit, lower financing

costs, greater access to supply chain inputs, established analytics capabilities, and access to

both captive ratepayers and data center customers. 24 These advantages signal NextEra’s

incumbents to further consolidate ownership of assets in PJM markets, further increasing

overall structural market power.

       NextEra touts some of these advantages as sources of potential cost savings to

customers, along with reliability, customer service, and $2.25 billion in bill credits. 31 These

claims are unprovable and are not guaranteed. For example, how will the Merger improve

the reliability of local utility service? There is no reason to expect that the merged profit

deterred competition from other developers of gas-fired generation, renewable energy,

deterred entry are not only a lack of price competition in the wholesale electricity market.

They also include the lack of growth opportunities for other providers of new generation for

data centers and the lack of new innovations spurred by competition to build merchant

generation and transmission assets. In addition, the Merger would create an incentive for

further increases in the concentration of asset ownership in PJM as existing large companies

will have an incentive to merge with or acquire other existing assets. These anticompetitive

       In addition to deterring other competitors, the Merger would remove a competitor

from the PJM market. NextEra’s purchase of Dominion’s access to the captive ratepayers of

generation and transmission, because NextEra’s competitors would know that NextEra faces

no risk of loss on its regulated investments, while they face competitive market risks.

competitor with a similar cost advantage. This is another way in which the Merger would

reduce the intensity of competition by both eliminating a competitor and deterring entry by

other competitors, especially smaller companies.

Introduction
This report was prepared by PJM’s Independent Market Monitor (IMM). The report
provides an assessment of the impact of the proposed merger of NextEra and Dominion
on the structure of the PJM energy and capacity markets, its direct impacts on static
measures of local and aggregate market power in both markets, and its impacts on
competition that are not captured by the traditional, static analysis. In conducting this
analysis, the IMM used market data including market shares and the results from the three
pivotal supplier test (TPS), the PJM test for structural market power. As part of the IMM
review, the IMM used market data to define the relevant markets and to examine the
effects of the proposed merger on those markets. The report finds that the
NextEra/Dominion merger (“Merger”) results in small increases in structural market
power based on existing generation assets and market definitions. Dominion has
substantial market power in PJM and in submarkets within PJM. NextEra would acquire
that market power as a result of the merger. More importantly, the Merger would remove
a significant competitor from the market for generation and transmission in PJM. NextEra
and Dominion are planning to build new large generation projects in PJM that, by
definition, are not included in the analysis of historical data. The IMM’s analysis, relying
on historical data, and the analysis based on historical data submitted by NextEra and
Dominion, cannot capture the actual effects of the Merger on competition in the PJM
market because they do not include the future plans of the companies, the trajectory of
load growth and consolidation in the industry, and the threat to future competition
created by the Merger. 1 The broader point is that, regardless of the details, no analysis of
historical data can address the impact of the Merger on post merger competition.
In conducting this analysis, the IMM addresses the Commission’s feedback in the May 1,
2026, Order regarding ArcLight’s purchase of KMC Thermo’s Brandywine plant. 2 The
IMM will continue to develop its approach to the analysis of mergers and acquisitions
under Section 203 of the FPA. The IMM used publicly available market data on frequently
binding constraints, using the Commission’s duration criterion, and market prices to
define a relevant submarket, as requested. 3 The IMM also used confidential PJM market
data, including market shares and the results from the three pivotal supplier test (TPS),
the PJM test for structural market power. The IMM used both public data and confidential

Summary of Market Power Findings
The IMM analyzed the effect of the NextEra/Dominion Merger on market power in the
PJM local energy markets and aggregate energy market using data for the 24 month
period from June 2024 through May 2026. The IMM analyzed the effect of the
NextEra/Dominion Merger on market power in the PJM Capacity Market using auction
data for the 2026/2027, 2027/2028, and 2028/2029 Base Residual Auctions.
The IMM finds small increases in structural market power, as determined by pivotal
supplier analysis, in the PJM Capacity Market, in the aggregate energy market, and in
energy market submarkets defined by local constraints that bind for more than five
percent of hours. The Delivered Price Test (“DPT”) analysis provided by applicants shows
no screen failures in the PJM market nor in the previously established submarkets that
include both Dominion and NextEra generation for which applicants submitted analysis,
which are AP South and PJM West submarkets. Applicants also found no screen failures
for the Dominion submarket and did not analyze the PJM East submarket.
There are frequently binding transmission constraints in the PJM market that limit the
flow of low marginal cost energy from the shale gas production regions of Pennsylvania
and West Virginia into Maryland and Virginia and neighboring areas of other states.
These frequently binding constraints, which the IMM identifies in this report, create a
significant submarket within PJM, which the IMM has identified as the Chesapeake
submarket. Dominion is the largest supplier and the dominant supplier in the Chesapeake
submarket, and the merger increases structural market power in the Chesapeake
submarket by a small amount relative to Dominion’s large position.
The IMM recommends that the transaction be rejected. No behavioral remedies are
sufficient to mitigate the market power created by the transaction or the acquisition of
market power in PJM by NextEra, which is likely to have different incentives than
Dominion currently does as a standalone Virginia power supplier.
However, if the transaction is to be approved, the transaction should only be approved
under specific behavioral remedies that would address the insufficiency of specific and
defined market power mitigation elements of PJM’s tariff. Each of the behavioral
conditions proposed by the IMM meets this Commission defined standard. None of the

All resources in PJM are required to submit at least one cost-based offer. Cost-based offers,
for a defined set of technologies, must include defined unit specific parameters, termed

based parameter limited schedule is used by PJM for committing generation resources
when a maximum emergency generation alert is declared. For capacity resources, the
price-based parameter limited schedule is used by PJM for committing generation
resources when hot weather alerts and cold weather alerts are declared. 16

Market Design
The Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) Capacity Market design was implemented in PJM on
June 1, 2007. The RPM Capacity Market is a forward-looking, annual, locational market,
with a must offer requirement for Existing Generation Capacity Resources and mandatory
participation by load, with performance incentives, that includes clear market power
mitigation rules and that permits the direct participation of demand-side resources.
Recent changes to the market power mitigation rules include ending the categorical
exemption from the must offer requirement for intermittent and storage resources. 51
Capacity storage resources include hydroelectric, flywheel and battery storage.
Intermittent resources include wind, solar, landfill gas, run of river hydroelectric, and
other renewable resources. Demand resources remain exempt from the must offer
requirement. In addition, the Commission recently approved the inclusion of standalone
CPQR offers with no net revenue offset and segmented offers based on CPQR, both of
which were opposed by the IMM as undermining market power mitigation. 52
Under RPM, capacity obligations are annual. Base Residual Auctions (BRA) are held for
delivery years that are three years in the future, although recent events have resulted in
shorter lead times for BRAs. Effective with the 2012/2013 Delivery Year, First, Second and
Third Incremental Auctions (IA) are held for each delivery year if there is time available. 53

The analysis of the impact of the NextEra/Dominion merger on the capacity market
examines the locational markets defined by the underlying economics of the market
including supply and demand curves and transmission constraints. Each transmission
zone is a Locational Deliverability Area (LDA) which can be a separate submarket if PJM

constraints and associated price separation in an auction. There are, in addition, several
defined subzonal LDAs, including PSEG North, DPL South, and ATSI Cleveland.

As in the energy market, to the extent that total RTO demand for capacity can be met

aggregate supply and demand curves. However, if the next increment of demand for
capacity in an LDA cannot be met by the next economic increment of total supply and
must be met by higher cost supply within the LDA, then the transmission constraint is
binding and there is a separate market created. That separate market is defined by the
incremental demand that must be met by capacity within the LDA and the higher cost
incremental supply within the LDA available to meet that demand.

The market for a constrained LDA is defined by the incremental supply available to meet
the incremental demand when locational incremental demand must be met by capacity
resources within the LDA. The RTO market is defined to include all supply that is not
incremental supply in a constrained LDA. The RTO market includes all MW that resulted
in the clearing price for the rest of RTO.
The three pivotal supplier (TPS) test measures the degree to which the incremental supply
from three suppliers of capacity is required in order to meet the incremental demand in
an LDA. In applying the TPS test in the capacity market, the relevant demand consists of
the incremental MW of capacity required to relieve a constraint or clear a market. The
relevant supply consists of the incremental MW of supply from generation resources
available to relieve the constraint or clear the market. The supply does not include
demand response resources.
